title: Serving runtime: reference architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes and runbooks
author: Priya Natarajan
summary: Comprehensive reference for Redwood's serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues, release notes, and operational runbooks used by the runtime team.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the runtime architecture, kernel scheduling rationale, profiling/playbook procedures, benchmarking suite usage, recent release notes, known issues, and day-2 runbooks for Redwood Inference's serving runtime. It is intended for engineers (runtime, infra, SRE) and on-call owners. The goal is to provide a single reference that covers design decisions, operational procedures, and repeatable measurement artifacts used to keep inference performant and reliable.

Contents
1) Runtime architecture summary
2) Kernel selection & scheduling
3) Profiling playbook (how-to)
4) Benchmarking suite (commands, interpretation)
5) Release notes (last 6 updates)
6) Known issues & mitigations
7) Runbooks & on-call procedures
8) Team wiki pointers and ownership

---

1) Runtime architecture summary

Short intro: Our serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine supporting LLMs with features for continuous batching, KV cache management, quantization-friendly execution, and pluggable kernel implementations. The runtime is split into three logical components:

- Frontend (http/gRPC layer, request normalization, auth) — service: inference-gateway
- Router & policy engine (smart routing, fallbacks) — service: inference-router
- Execution plane (device drivers, kernel execution, KV cache) — service: inference-executor

Key guarantees and SLOs:
- 99.95% uptime for inference-gateway and inference-router (per-region)
- Median p50 token latency target: < 10ms for short-context (< 128 tokens) workloads on dedicated T4/T4x clusters; p99 < 200ms for similar workloads
- Batch tail SLO: 95th percentile batch wait < 7ms during normal load windows
- Cost SLO (internal): avg tokens/sec per GPU >= target baseline per model profile (see benchmarking section)

Deployment model notes:
- Hosted API: scaled multi-tenant pools with prefix caching and model-variant fallbacks
- Dedicated: reserved GPU pools with tenant pinning and stricter isolation
- Private: packaged runtime + operator manifests with required kernel modules and KMS integration

Ownership: serving-runtime team (runtime@redwood.internal)

---

2) Kernel selection & scheduling

Rationale: Different kernels (attention math, matmul implementations, fused ops) have tradeoffs between latency, memory footprint, and throughput. Kernel selection is decided by: model architecture, sequence length distribution, batch size distribution, and hardware profile (SM count, memory, tensor core availability).

Policy summary:
- Default kernel profile is chosen at model onboarding using the model-onboarding harness (see model-onboarding docs).
- Runtime uses a two-tier selection: compile-time candidate set and runtime selector that may switch kernels when sequence-length or batch-size distributions cross thresholds.
- Kernel fallback policy: if an optimized kernel raises OOMs or diverges numerically, the runtime falls back to a numerically-safe kernel and records a kernel-fallback event in telemetry.

Scheduling notes (execution-executor):
- Continuous batching: worker threads assemble micro-batches up to N tokens or T milliseconds (configurable per pool)
- Preemption: high-priority low-latency requests (priority=rt) can preempt batching windows via fast-path execution (configurable token budget)
- Affinity: executor assigns CUDA contexts with CPU core affinity to limit PCIe contention; use cpuset configs in the node agent (example below)

Example node agent affinity config (YAML):

node_agent_affinity: |
  gpu0: "cpuset=0-7"
  gpu1: "cpuset=8-15"
  metrics_poll_interval_ms: 1000

Kernel tuning knobs (common):
- tile_size (integer) — influences shared memory tiling for matmul
- fp16_accumulation (boolean) — enable fp16 accumulation paths to reduce memory
- kv_cache_alignment (integer) — align KV cache to reduce fragmentation

Telemetry to track kernel health:
- kernel_fallback.count (incremental)
- kernel_latency_ms.{kernel_name}.p50/p95/p99
- kernel_memory_bytes.{kernel_name}.max

---

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Purpose: produce reproducible traces and profiles to diagnose latency regressions, memory growth, and batch formation issues. Use this playbook for on-call escalations and pre-release performance validation.

Pre-steps: ensure access to the profiling cluster (tag: profiling) and that the target model is pinned to a non-shared pool.

Checklist: 
1. Reproduce: capture representative request(s) as HAR or recorded JSON payloads from production traces (route: /v1/infer).
2. Baseline: run the benchmark harness (see section 4) with the same payloads to establish a clean profile.
3. Live profile: enable per-request tracing for the tenant for a short window (30s) — command: `curl -X POST https://control-plane/api/v1/tracing/tenants/{tenant}/enable?duration=30s`
4. Collect sysprof & CUPTI traces on executor node:
   - SSH to node: ssh -A ops@executor-node-123
   - Start system profile: `sudo /opt/redwood/tools/run_sysprof.sh --pid $(pgrep inference-executor) --out /tmp/prof`
   - Start CUPTI: `sudo nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys_profile --force --sampling on --trace="cuda,cuda_memory" --duration=30s --target-pid $(pgrep inference-executor)`
5. Collect runtime logs, kernel events, and telemetry for the same time window (use trace_id correlation).
6. Analyze: use the profiling notebook (GCS: gs://redwood-infra/profiling/notebooks/runtime-analysis.ipynb) to load nsys and sysprof outputs. Watch for:
   - Long mutex holds (>50ms) in batcher threads
   - KV cache thrashing (continuous eviction logs)
   - Kernel stalls or repeated OOM fallbacks

Quick diagnostic commands:
- Top-level latency breakdown (via metrics api): `curl -s https://metrics.internal/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.99,sum(rate(inference_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le,route))`
- Active batch sizes: `curl https://executor.internal/debug/batches`

Postmortem attachments: include raw nsys .qdrep, system profile tarball, trace IDs, and a short hypothesis section (3 bullet max).

---

4) Benchmarking suite (commands, interpretation)

Purpose: measure throughput (tokens/sec/GPU), latency distributions, memory usage, and cost baselines for model profiles. Benchmarks are used for onboarding, release gating, and capacity planning.

Quick start (local harness):
- Checkout: `git clone git@repo:redwood/serving-benchmarks.git`
- Install: `pip install -r requirements.txt`
- Run a single-model latency run: `./benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --model /models/llama-3-7b --mode latency --batch_sizes 1 2 4 --seq_lengths 64 128`
- Run an end-to-end throughput test (multi-client): `./benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --model /models/llama-3-7b --mode throughput --clients 32 --duration 300`

Benchmark outputs (CSV + JSON):
- tokens_per_sec_per_gpu (float)
- latency_ms.{p50,p95,p99} (ms)
- memory_peak_mb (MB)
- batch_formation_stats (avg_size, wait_ms)

Interpreting results:
- If p99 latency increases > 2x from baseline, fail the gating check and start profiling playbook.
- If tokens_per_sec_per_gpu < baseline -10%, check kernel selection, quantization profile, and batcher behavior.

Example baseline table (put in README for each model profile):
| model | hardware | tokens/sec/GPU | p50(ms) | p99(ms) | notes |
| llama-3-7b | T4x (16GB) | 11,200 | 8.5 | 120 | default fq8 quant profile |
| llama-3-13b | A10G | 6,400 | 12 | 250 | use fused attention kernel v2 |

Automated nightly benchmarks:
- CI: nightly-bench job executes core model profiles and pushes results to BigTable and to dashboards (grafana board: runtime-bench). Alerts fire if regressions exceed configured thresholds.

5) Release notes (recent items)

2029-10-28 — release v2029.10.28
- Kernel: rolled out fused-attention-v2 for 13B LLaMA family. Observed 18% throughput uplift and 12% p99 reduction on A10G pools.
- Scheduling: added preemption fast-path for priority=rt; default budget 5 tokens.
- Bugfix: fixed memory leak in KV cache eviction when using remote backing store.

2029-07-11 — release v2029.07.11
- Benchmarking: added multi-client jitter tests to the harness.
- Telemetry: added kernel_fallback.* metrics and alerts.

2028-12-05 — release v2028.12.05
- Runtime: introduced continuous-batching v1.3 with adaptive wait timers.
- Ops: node agent added cpuset enforcement for executor pods.

6) Known issues & mitigations

1) Symptom: Occasional p99 spike correlated with mixed sequence lengths.
   - Root cause: Batcher assembles long+short sequences into same micro-batch causing stragglers.
   - Mitigation: Enable sequence-length bucketing for affected pools (config flag: enable_length_bucketing=true).
   - Long-term: proposing an async micro-batching redesign (ADR ID: 2029-02-batching).

2) Symptom: Kernel fallback churn causing small correctness diffs in decoded tokens.
   - Root cause: Some optimized kernels use relaxed fp16 accumulation paths that differ numerically from fallback kernel.
   - Mitigation: Mark model profiles with strict_numeric=true to force safe kernel selection on sensitive tenants. Telemetry will emit kernel_numeric_diff.rate.

3) Symptom: OOMs during large-batch throughput tests on older A100 nodes.
   - Mitigation: Deploy quantization-profile fq8 for these nodes or cap batch_size in node profile.

4) Symptom: Profiling overhead distorts timings when sysprof runs concurrently with clients.
   - Mitigation: use isolated profiling cluster or run short-duration captures. Record a baseline run without profiling enabled for comparison.

---

7) Runbooks & on-call procedures

Runbook: High p99 latency on inference-gateway
1. Pager triggers: latency-alert-high-p99 (threshold: p99 > 2x baseline for 5m).
2. Triage: check grafana board runtime-latency -> identify affected routes/models.
3. Check upstream router: `kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=inference-router` and review `router.log` for fallback events.
4. If fallback events present, escalate to runtime lead and run profiling playbook steps 1-5.
5. Temporary mitigation: redirect traffic to secondary region or raise autoscale target for dedicated pools.

Runbook: Executor OOMs
1. Alert: executor-oom (per-node).
2. Inspect: `kubectl -n inference logs <executor-pod> | grep -i oom`
3. If OOM is KV cache related, run: `curl -X POST https://control-plane/api/v1/pools/{pool}/evict-kv-cache?percentage=20`
4. If persistent, cordon node and migrate pods: `kubectl cordon <node>` then `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets`
5. Post-incident: run benchmarking suite to reproduce and capture telemetry.

Escalation contacts: runtime on-call (rotation link: https://oncall.redwood.internal/runtime), execution engineers: Ethan Zhang, Marisol Vega.

Appendices
A) Example telemetry query (Prometheus):
```
sum(rate(kernel_fallback_count[5m])) by (kernel_name)
```
B) Example eviction command (control-plane API):
```
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://control-plane/api/v1/pools/my-pool/evict-kv-cache -d '{"percentage":20}'
```
C) Templates: attach nsys trace and postmortem template to any incident record.

If you have questions or need help executing the playbook, contact the runtime on-call rotation or open a ticket in the runtime board (project: INF-RUNTIME).
